This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup , in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

Kyrgyzstan’s progress in creating an inclusive and accessible environment for people with disabilities remains limited after seven years of ratifying the United Nations (UN) Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities in 2019. Despite a legal responsibility to undertake measures that would remove legal and physical barriers and help people with disabilities lead independent social and economic lives, the government has not prioritized this commitment at the level requested by the country’s disabled community. In such circumstances, holding the government accountable requires proof of how much physical infrastructure remains inaccessible for the more than 218,000 people with disabilities in the country — about three percent of the population.

One of the organizations leading this effort in Kyrgyzstan is the public fund “Oasis” , which is documenting the level of physical inaccessibility in the capital, Bishkek, with the help of people with disabilities who are auditing objects through their real-life experiences. Global Voices conducted a written interview with Oasis to learn about this work, which is being carried out under the Digital Sparks project. The interview has been edited for clarity and brevity. Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Sparks project.

Oasis (O): Founded in 2003, Oasis is a Kyrgyz civil society organization working to build inclusive communities where everyone can participate and reach their full potential. We joined the project because we know that it is not possible to build an inclusive city without listening to the people navigating its barriers every day. In Bishkek, we saw accessibility discussed through policies and assumptions, while lived experiences remained largely invisible. We wanted to change that to make exclusion visible, measurable, and impossible to overlook with the help of data. Digital Sparks helped us build the Oasis Data Lab, bringing together citizen-generated data, digital mapping, storytelling, and advocacy.

Our goal was not simply to create a map, but to build a bridge between lived experience and public decision-making, turning everyday barriers into evidence for change. GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project? O: The project grew from a practical problem: people with disabilities face barriers across Bishkek, but these barriers were not being systematically documented. Public transport, entrances, ramps, toilets, signage, and other parts of the urban environment can make everyday participation difficult. Yet without reliable and regularly updated data, these problems remain easy to overlook.

Kyrgyzstan ratified the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities in 2019, but there is still a gap between formal commitments and everyday accessibility. Previous assessments were limited and did not create a living public record that could be used to monitor progress. We therefore started from a simple principle: before accessibility can be improved, it has to be measured. And the people who experience these barriers every day should be directly involved in producing that evidence. GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?

O: Through Digital Sparks, we developed Oasis Data Lab into a more structured space for digital civic participation. We brought together more than 30 young people, including people with physical disabilities, blind and low-vision participants, deaf participants, social activists, and urban experts. We organized workshops on disability rights, inclusivity, digital advocacy, data collection, mapping, and storytelling. A major practical change was integrating UrbanEyes into our work. Through the application, participants can assess buildings using geolocation, photographs, questionnaires, and standardized accessibility indicators. The web platform then visualizes this information through an interactive map, filters, heat maps, and accessibility indices.

Most importantly, the project moved us from collecting individual complaints toward creating structured, comparable civic data that can support advocacy, dialogue with authorities, and evidence-based urban planning. GV: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples. O: One of the biggest impacts has been the shift in how participants are positioned: not simply as beneficiaries, but as researchers, digital monitors, and civic actors. Participants have already assessed 350 buildings across Bishkek and transformed their observations into geo-referenced data for the city’s accessibility map.

The results show the scale of the problem clearly: 60.3 percent of assessed buildings had a ramp-related barrier, either because there was no ramp or because the existing ramp was difficult or unsuitable to use. The project also allows participants to compare accessibility across districts and types of buildings, rather than relying only on individual complaints. Just as importantly, participants are learning to communicate findings through digital storytelling and advocacy. Their lived experience is becoming structured evidence that can be presented directly to decision-makers and used to argue for concrete improvements.

GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed, thanks to your participation in the project? O: The project changed our understanding of digital democracy. We previously saw digital tools mainly as instruments for research, communication, and advocacy. Digital Sparks helped us understand their deeper democratic potential: digital democracy can change not only how information is shared, but who gets to produce it, whose voices are visible, and who participates in decision-making. Participatory mapping showed that technology can shift evidence production closer to communities themselves. People can document the barriers they experience, make them visible, and use this evidence to demand change.

We also learned that digital democracy must be accessible, safe, and rights-based. More importantly, we realized that as society becomes increasingly digital, traditional forms of participation alone are no longer enough. Digital democracy offers an opportunity to make civic participation more inclusive, responsive, and effective. GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project? O: Our most valuable lesson is that “Nothing About Us Without Us” should apply not only to policymaking, but also to the evidence on which policy is based. Lived experience can reveal things that a conventional audit may miss.

A checklist may show that a building has a ramp, while a wheelchair user can show that the ramp is too steep, slippery, too narrow, lacks handrails, or still does not allow independent access. We also learned that data must remain dynamic. Accessibility cannot be measured once and considered solved; information needs to be updated and connected to advocacy. Finally, data alone does not create change. Its value comes from combining reliable evidence with storytelling, community leadership, public communication, and structured dialogue with institutions. That combination is what turns information into civic power. GV: What comes next?

How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community? O: Our next step is to make Oasis Data Lab a long-term civic innovation and evidence hub rather than a one-time project. We plan to continue developing the UrbanEyes app and Bishkek’s Accessibility Map , regularly updating the data and using it to identify priority areas and support public accountability. We also intend to use the findings in dialogue with Bishkek’s Mayor’s Office, the Ministry of Labour, Social Protection and Migration, civil society, businesses, and other stakeholders.

The data can help identify areas requiring urgent improvement and support more informed infrastructure planning and budgeting. Participants will be encouraged to continue contributing data, producing digital stories, and sharing their skills with other young advocates. In the longer term, we want to adapt this model to other regions, especially rural ones.

Forty-six days later, just when Nepal was trying to recover from the Bhotekoshi flash flood , which struck the Nepal–Tibet border regions, affecting Rasuwa and Nuwakot, another landslide-induced flood hit Chumnubri, Gorkha, on October 11, 2026. This latest disaster has added to the wounds of communities who live in the shadow of natural hazards, where uncertainty and fear are daily realities.

The climate-related disaster in Nuwakot has devastated a once-popular tourist landscape, destroying its natural beauty and economic opportunities, with settlements heartbreakingly reduced to rubble and vital infrastructure , including roads, bridges and hydro-power facilities, washed away. The full death toll remains officially unconfirmed. Survivors still come to search for their belongings in Devighatm, Nuwakot District. Image via Susmita Aryal on October 7, 2026. Used with permission. But an uncomfortable truth lies behind the devastation: The human cost of such disasters often goes ignored. Behind the statistics are stories of broken dreams, lost livelihoods, buried memories.

There are families trying to stay alive without their loved ones, communities faced with an uncertain future, and countless people trying to make lives reconnect and rebuild from what little is left. The task of rebuilding is huge. The damage is not only to homes, roads and bridges, but also to farms and local businesses. Kyodo News reports via AP that 7,500 homes were damaged or completely destroyed, with costs of recovery hitting USD 4.77 billion. The government has now moved from emergency relief to rehabilitation and reconstruction and has also acknowledged the risks posed by possible glacial outburst floods ( GLOFs ) and other hazards.

The destruction of bridges and transport links has made surviving communities vulnerable and slowed reconstruction, exposing residents to further risk. Buildings left standing, and homes left empty in the Bidur Municipality in Nuwakot District. Image via Susmita Aryal on October 7, 2026. Used with permission. To this end, joint efforts are underway to rebuild damaged infrastructure and restore vital services. But pledged assistance is not the same as money that has actually been received and delivered to affected communities. Nepal’s Ministry of Finance’s foreign assistance tracker shows that Nepal has received USD 24.89 million in disaster relief funds.

Such tracking can help bring transparency to the collection and distribution of aid. The Prime Minister's Office separately reported that USD 50.47 million of assistance (cash, materials, and teams) had been pledged. No formal update has been given on the implementation of longer-term reconstruction plans. Most of the aid is still going to meet immediate needs like medical aid, food, and temporary shelters, such as tents. What are houses without their people called? Photo featuring reporter Susmita Aryal. Photo from Bidur Municipality in Nuwakot District via Maya Devi Aryal on October 7, 2026. Used with permission. Many affected communities remain far from rebuilt infrastructure and restored livelihoods.

India, China, the United States, and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) are providing assistance, and the Asian Development Bank and other international financial institutions have committed funds . Yet recovery is likely to progress unevenly. The challenge for affected communities is not just to rebuild what was lost but to restore livelihoods, public services and a sense of security in the face of recurring environmental hazards. pages.text: There has been welcome diplomatic progress in recent months. But for civilians in eastern DRC, that progress has yet to translate into greater security. More than 26 million people in DRC face acute food insecurity, including 3.6 million at emergency levels. Conflict and displacement are compounding the effects of the Ebola outbreak and climate-related shocks. The United Kingdom continues to support the humanitarian response, including our assistance to the Ebola response. But all parties must guarantee safe, rapid, and unhindered humanitarian access, and remove obstacles to the delivery of lifesaving assistance.

Second, we welcome progress through the Doha and Washington processes, including recent EJVM+ deployments with the support of MONUSCO, alongside ongoing African Union-led mediation efforts. To achieve lasting peace, agreements and mechanisms must now deliver tangible improvements for people on the ground. We call on all parties to cease hostilities, implement their commitments in full, and engage constructively and in good faith with the peace processes. The Washington, Doha and African Union-led processes must reinforce one another, with clear coordination and African ownership. Progress also depends on those working for peace being able to do their jobs.

All parties must respect MONUSCO’s mandate and guarantee the Mission the freedom of movement that it needs. And all parties must fully adhere to their obligations under international humanitarian law, including on the protection of civilians. The increasing use of drones, heavy artillery, and explosive weaponry in populated areas is increasing the threat to civilians and civilian infrastructure. Third, the ongoing illicit exploitation and trafficking of critical minerals in the region sustains armed groups, undermines trust, and deprives communities of legitimate development. We support the Secretary-General’s call for strengthening the Regional Certification Mechanism. And we encourage regional and international actors to work together to ensure stronger traceability and certification mechanisms.

The development of critical minerals should reach local communities, not drive conflicts. President, sustained diplomacy has created an opportunity for progress. But its measure will be on what changes on the ground: whether civilians are safer, humanitarian assistance can reach those who need it, and the parties fulfil the commitments that they have made. We urge all parties and regional leaders to turn the present diplomatic momentum into lasting peace.

pages.text: Dear Chair, as this is the first formal statement that the United Kingdom has made to the Committee in this session, before I begin, I wanted to place on record my delegation’s congratulations to you and members of the Bureau on your election. We look forward to working productively with you throughout this session. As the Committee has heard before, the United Kingdom has a modern relationship with all of its Overseas Territories based on partnership; on shared values; and on the right of the people of each Territory to choose to remain British or not.

The United Kingdom Overseas Territories are self-governing, subject only to the UK retaining powers to carry out its obligations under international law. We have a close bilateral relationship with each Territory, and the United Kingdom’s and Overseas Territory Governments hold a Joint Ministerial Council each year to monitor and drive forward collective priorities for action in the spirit of partnership, considering the uniqueness and diversity of each Territory. We are committed to supporting the Territories on their priorities, including environmental protection, and carrying out our constitutional responsibilities, including guaranteeing security.

Indeed, we consider the Territories to be a core part of the UK “homeland” when it comes to our defence and security responsibilities. Across the Territories, we provide financial and practical support to build local capacity and resilience, where it is needed. Our near £100m programme for reconstruction after Hurricane Irma hit Anguilla is now complete. And in other Territories, a new port now operational on Saint Helena, a new hospital nearing construction on Montserrat, new coastal radars operational on Turks & Caicos. I will address specific points relating to three of the United Kingdom’s Overseas Territories.

The United Kingdom is clear that the people of Gibraltar enjoy the right to self-determination, in accordance with the Charter of the United Nations. The 2006 Gibraltar Constitution, which was endorsed in a referendum by the people of Gibraltar, provides for a modern and mature partnership between Gibraltar and the United Kingdom. It is only right, therefore, that the Committee has heard directly from the Chief Minister of Gibraltar, as the elected representative of its people. The United Kingdom restates its longstanding commitment to the people of Gibraltar.

The United Kingdom will not enter into arrangements under which the people of Gibraltar would pass under the sovereignty of another state against their freely and democratically expressed wishes. Nor will we ever enter into a process of sovereignty negotiations with which Gibraltar is not content. The United Kingdom welcomes the Agreement in respect of Gibraltar between the European Union and the United Kingdom, signed in Brussels on 14 July 2026.

The Agreement, in which the United Kingdom worked side by side with the Government of Gibraltar, is without prejudice to the respective legal positions of the United Kingdom and Spain with regard to sovereignty and jurisdiction, and reaffirms that those positions remain unchanged. But it also reflects a new era of cooperation, trust, and respect between the United Kingdom, the European Union, Spain, and Gibraltar. The United Kingdom encourages all parties to build on this positive momentum in order to further strengthen cooperation and foster a mutually beneficial relationship based on solidarity, dialogue, and shared prosperity.

The United Kingdom has no doubt about its sovereignty over both the Falkland Islands, and South Georgia, and the South Sandwich Islands, and their surrounding maritime areas. Nor do we have any doubt about the Falkland Islanders’ right of self-determination. This is enshrined in the UN Charter and in Article One of both UN covenants on human rights, by virtue of which they are free to determine their political status and pursue their economic, social, and cultural development.

In the 2013 referendum, which was conducted in line with international standards and was observed by independent, international observers, 99.8 per cent of those who voted wanted to remain their current status as a British Overseas Territory. Argentina’s decision to initiate arbitration against the United Kingdom under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) is the latest attempt to undermine the rights and livelihoods of the people of the Falkland Islands. The people of the Falkland Islands have freely and democratically chosen their future, and they have every right to develop and manage their natural resources without intimidation, coercion, or interference from others.

Hydrocarbon activities on the Falkland Islands continental shelf are regulated under Falkland Islands law and conducted in full accordance with international law, including UNCLOS. The United Kingdom will continue to stand shoulder-to-shoulder with the Falkland Islands Government and the Falkland Islanders. We will robustly defend their wishes, their economy, and their right to determine their own future. There is no change to the United Kingdom’s long-standing position. Where it is the clear and constitutionally expressed will of the British Virgin Islanders to pursue independence, the United Kingdom Government will meet its obligations to help the Territory achieve it.

For as long as the British Virgin Islands remains an Overseas Territory, the United Kingdom is committed to working in partnership with the BVI Government to deliver in the interests of all its people. We have been holding constructive talks on constitutional reform in that spirit, and will keep the Committee informed of the outcome of those talks. Chair, in conclusion, the United Kingdom remains committed to respecting and defending the right of the people of each Territory to determine their own future, in line with the UN Charter.
And let me also reassure you that the United Kingdom will continue to carry out our responsibilities as part of our modern partnership with each of the territories.

pages.text: The European Centre for Democratic Resilience has taken an important step towards involving candidate countries and potential candidates in its work. In the margins of the General Affairs Council in Luxembourg on 13 October, EU ministers endorsed the association of Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Moldova, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Serbia and Ukraine, together with Kosovo * .

Ministers discussed potential areas of cooperation with enlargement partners in future projects, including developing common concepts and methodologies for detection of foreign information manipulation and interference (FIMI), measuring democratic resilience, engaging in tabletop crisis management exercises, and supporting the safety of democratic life through dedicated trainings on the protection of journalists, civil society organisations, fact-checkers and politicians. Member States can now invite enlargement partners to propose, co-lead and participate in some of the Centre’s projects.

The participation of enlargement partners broadens the Centre’s practical cooperation and contributes to its core objectives to collectively improve the capacity to detect and anticipate threats to democratic resilience in Europe and its neighbourhood, to develop well-coordinated approaches and strengthen rapid response capacity, and to empower citizens, civil society and institutions to contribute towards democratic resilience. The Centre, which was officially launched on 24 February 2026, is already delivering several concrete projects with Member States. In early September, a Training of the Trainers programme was rolled out with the Swedish Psychological Defence Agency, designed to help upskill government officials across Member States and strengthen whole-of-government and whole-of-society preparedness.

The Centre has also launched the pilot phase of the Stakeholder Platform to test how the Centre can develop concrete projects for strengthening democratic resilience together with independent civil society organisations, media, fact-checkers, researchers, and media literacy professionals from across the EU. * This designation is without prejudice to positions on status, and is in line with UNSCR 1244/1999 and the ICJ Opinion on the Kosovo declaration of independence.

pages.text: The United Kingdom welcomes the progress Syria has made in recent months. President Sharaa’s participation during the UN General Assembly High-Level Week was an important demonstration of Syria’s continued engagement with international partners, as it works towards a more stable and prosperous future. Many Syrians continue to face significant economic hardship, including rising living costs and pressure on household incomes. Political progress must increasingly be accompanied by tangible improvements in people’s lives. We therefore welcome the Syrian government’s efforts to attract investment, strengthen regional economic ties and support reconstruction and livelihoods.

The international community should continue to support measures that restore economic opportunity, improve basic services and create the conditions for sustainable recovery, including for displaced Syrians to return home. For our part, the United Kingdom is committed to supporting Syria’s recovery. We have allocated $90 million this financial year, including support for education, entrepreneurship, agriculture and livelihoods. This will help create jobs, address continuing humanitarian needs and build confidence in Syria’s future. Second, recent reports of sectarian tensions and violence underline the importance of ensuring that Syria’s political progress remains inclusive.

Lasting stability depends on all Syrians having confidence that their rights and security will be protected and that they have a stake in their country’s future. The United Kingdom continues to emphasise the importance of inclusive governance, meaningful participation by all communities, and credible transitional justice processes. Accountability and equal protection are essential to building trust and preventing renewed instability. Third, respect for Syria’s sovereignty and territorial integrity remains essential for long-term stability, political progress and economic recovery. In that regard, I reaffirm the United Kingdom’s longstanding position that we consider the Golan Heights to be occupied Syrian territory.

President, the progress achieved so far is real, but it is not yet secure. The task now is to translate political progress into economic opportunity, inclusive governance and lasting stability for all Syrians. The United Kingdom will continue to support that effort.

pages.text: We, the Foreign Ministers of Australia, Canada, France and the United Kingdom deeply regret the Palestinian President’s decision to postpone the Palestinian Legislative Council elections as well as the Presidential elections to September 2027. Nearly two decades have passed since the last Palestinian Legislative Council elections and five years since the planned 2021 elections were postponed. An entire generation of Palestinians has reached adulthood without the opportunity to choose their elected representatives. This delay will be deeply disappointing and once again deprive Palestinians of the opportunity to vote and will further erode public confidence in democratic institutions.

We acknowledge that significant challenges and impediments have affected the ability to conduct elections in a manner fully consistent with international standards and with the participation of all eligible Palestinians. We commend the important work of the Central Elections Commission in advancing practical preparations to address these challenges and facilitate voter participation. Credible elections are an important element of the commitment that President Abbas and the Palestinian Authority made to reform, including democratic renewal and accountable governance, and are in line with the June 2025 New York Declaration.

Strengthening Palestinian governance is essential to continue building the institutional foundations of a viable two-state solution, which is the only path to lasting peace and security for both Israel and Palestine. As longstanding supporters of Palestinian self-determination, we call on the Palestinian Authority to reconsider the decision to postpone elections and to take the necessary steps to hold legislative and presidential elections, without further delay. We will continue to support efforts to deliver on these elections. We reiterate our call on Israel to refrain from actions that could impede the conduct of elections, including the practical arrangements necessary for all Palestinians to participate.

Lastly, we reiterate our longstanding position that Hamas can have no role in the future governance of Palestine. Email the FCDO Newsdesk (monitored 24 hours a day) in the first instance, and we will respond as soon as possible.

Used with permission A new poetry anthology features writers of Chabacano, one of the Philippines’ 170 languages, which is widely spoken in the southernmost city of Zamboanga, and stands out as Asia’s only Spanish-based creole language. The Philippines was a colony of Spain for more than three centuries, but the Spanish language was only used by the elite, friars, and colonial rulers. Only in Zamboanga did a Spanish-based creole language develop. In 2018, Global Voices featured Bien Chabacano , a blog dedicated to promoting and documenting Chavacano de Zamboanga.

Its creator, Jerome Herrera, launched a book project this year by inviting writers to submit poems to be compiled in an anthology. This led to the launch of the “ Sombra y Luz ” book in July, featuring 23 poems by 10 authors. The poems are mainly about love, family, and Zamboangueño identity. Herrera said , “The project highlights not only the continued vitality of Chavacano as a literary language, but also the efforts of its speakers to create new literature and preserve the language through writing.” He added that the book title aims to convey a message of contrast about the changes in Zamboanga City.

The book cover also provides a nostalgic reference to the flowers that decorated the city in the past. The cover features an American-era style lamppost that can be seen along the Zamboanga boulevard. The cover also features bougainvilleas which my dad tells me were ubiquitous in Zamboanga City back when it was known as the Ciudad de Flores. Herrera’s poem in the anthology mentions flowers and birds that enrich life in the city. Maga pajaro que ta vola-vola, Na maga rama de pono ta queda, Alegre con uno y otro ta grita-grita, Twit! Twit! Twit! Entero el dia. Mio pueblo Ciudad de Zamboanga, Ciudad de Flores que llama.

De noche mucho pajaro ay columbra, Na maga cable de corriente ta esta. Birds that fly and flutter freely, Perched upon the branches of trees, Singing and calling each other joyfully, Tweet! Tweet! Tweet! All day long. Oh, my beloved City of Zamboanga, City of Flowers, they call you. At night, many birds can be found, Sitting on wires, that’s what they do. In an interview with Global Voices, Herrera noted the heavy use of Spanish words in the selected poems: …there is a lot of debate with regards to what Chabacano poetry should look like.

For some, they like it with a lot of Spanish words and for others, they like it to be exactly as how Chabacano appears in everyday conversations. Most of the poems submitted leaned heavily on Spanish words, I think primarily because Chabacano writers rely on Spanish words to make their works sound more formal as well as more poetic. Since it’s poetry, I thought that it was alright to present Chabacano in an idealistic manner. He added that the anthology seeks to encourage more people to accept the various ways that Chabacano is used. For a very long time, people have been putting Chabacano inside a box.

I hope that these books open up conversations regarding Chabacano literature and make people receptive to different kinds of writing styles in Chabacano. This approach is evident in the poem “Escribi Chavacano, Conversa Chabacano,” which celebrates Chabacano as a living language. Through references to poems, essays, fables, and the stories passed down by elders, the author reminds readers that the language continues to thrive when it is written, spoken, and shared with others. The title itself is noteworthy for its use of both Chavacano and Chabacano, reflecting the coexistence of two accepted spellings of the language.

In doing so, the poem highlights not only the importance of preserving Chabacano, but also the richness and diversity of its written tradition. Herrera’s interview with Asymptote Journal noted the challenge of finding Chabacano contributors, and his hope that the book project can lead to more literary initiatives. The biggest challenge is keeping the momentum going, since it’s hard to find Chavacano poets. Even so, I hope this anthology is just the beginning and that we’ll be able to publish a second volume in the future.

pages.text: Ukrainians facing another winter of blackouts and freezing temperatures will see the Foreign Secretary back President Zelenskyy’s support for an energy ceasefire at the Warsaw Security Forum today (Tuesday 13 October). As Ukraine continues to take steps towards peace, Russia once again looks to weaponise winter and plunge communities into darkness. In the past week alone, Russia has mounted 200 attacks against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. This is part of a wider pattern of Russian aggression, with the Kremlin firing 1,450 bombs and 1,600 drones at Ukraine in the same time period.

The future of how Europe takes on growing hybrid attacks from hostile states will also be top of the agenda during a panel event where the Foreign Secretary will speak alongside Foreign Ministers of Poland, Germany and Norway. The Foreign Secretary is expected to emphasise that Russian actions pose an immediate and urgent threat to the British way of life and will call on European partners to mobilise economic, industrial and political strength with greater purpose to protect their people, interests and way of life. Russia’s attempts to disrupt Europe pose an immediate threat to UK security and prosperity.

These are deliberate threats to destabilise the systems that deliver growth and security for Brits, the UK’s new National Centre for Information Defence, and new partnership with Germany to tackle hybrid threats, will strengthen the UK’s defences against these attempts to threaten our security in our country and across the continent. These steps are being matched by the largest sustained increase in defence spending since the Cold War, with the UK investing more than £300 billion over the next four years. Ahead of the Forum, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said: As Putin’s war drags on, Russia’s ambitions have reached far beyond Ukraine’s borders.

From almost weekly drone incursions along NATO’s eastern flank to cyber-attacks and sabotage targeting critical infrastructure, Moscow’s hybrid aggression is being felt across Europe, with Poland on the frontline. Russia’s tactics have the real potential to impact British daily life, as their attempts at hybrid sabotage increasingly target energy, infrastructure and the information space. In December 2025, a Russian attack on Poland’s energy grid came close to leaving half a million people without power in the depths of winter, while a train sabotage the previous month narrowly avoided mass casualties.

In Poland, the Foreign Secretary has met with Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski where he underlined the UK’s solidarity with Poland as they confront Russian threats head-on. They discussed how the UK and Poland Northolt Treaty , signed earlier this year, has deepened cooperation across defence, security and economic resilience, and strengthens joint action to tackle hybrid activities, including cyber and sabotage attacks. The Foreign Secretary’s approach to foreign policy is driven by his values, values rooted in his family’s history. In Warsaw, the Foreign Secretary has encountered that history first hand in a visit to the Jewish Historical Institute.
The Foreign Secretary met with the Director, Dr Michał Trębacz, and archivist Aleksandra Szarapanowska, who were able to show the Foreign Secretary some archives directly related to his family.

pages.text: A Balli Walirafudhu handover ceremony held by the Borana Oromo people in Southern Ethiopia and northern Kenya. They have long practiced rotational, peaceful leadership transfer, known as the Borana Gadaa system. Photo used with permission. This article by Diba Kosi Bilinga was originally published by Peace News Network on July 20, 2026. An edited version is being republished on Global Voices under a content partnership agreement. Every election season, much of Africa braces itself. In some cases, incumbents amend constitutions to erase term limits, and citizens wait to see whether power will change hands at the ballot box or in the streets.

The pattern repeats: disputed results , ethnic mobilization, coups , or leaders who refuse to leave . Yet in the rangelands of southern Ethiopia and northern Kenya, the Borana Oromo people have long practiced rotational, peacefully transferred leadership. Known as the Borana Gadaa system, UNESCO inscribed it in 2016 as an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity that regulates political and social life, resolves conflict, and protects women’s rights.

This article asks a question: What can African leaders, electoral commissions, political parties, and citizens learn from a governance model that has quietly rotated power every eight years for generations, without coups, without third-term referenda, and without the bloodshed that so often accompanies modern African elections? Borana leadership rotates on a fixed eight-year cycle among five Gogeessas (parties). Each governs for one Gadaa period, then hands over power, returning to the first after 40 years — a rotation built into the structure itself. Compare this to Africa’s modern pattern.

Human Rights Watch (HRW) director Ida Sawyer describes a “constitutional coup” pattern: leaders who cannot win re-election simply rewrite the laws to get their way. Cameroon’s Paul Biya erased term limits in 2008 and has ruled since 1982; Uganda’s Museveni scrapped his in 2005 ; Rwanda, Burundi, Togo, Djibouti, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) have each amended their constitutions to extend a president’s tenure. Gadaa’s lesson is structural: When a time limit is built into the system itself, rather than a leader’s promise, departure never has to be settled by force. Gadaa systems treat leadership as something built over decades, not switched on by an election.

Members pass through age-grades from childhood, absorbing law, custom, and ritual responsibility long before they are eligible to lead — knowledge oral historians formally transmit across generations. Most African political systems do the opposite: Candidates are selected first, and asked whether they are fit to govern only afterward. Patronage, money, and ethnic arithmetic often outweigh demonstrated understanding of law or public finance, producing leaders who improvise governance while learning on the job. The lesson for African parties and civic institutions: Build structured pipelines — in local councils, youth wings, and civil service — that expose future leaders to responsibility long before a national mandate.

Under the Gadaa system, at the Balli Walirafudhu handover ceremony, authority passes from the outgoing ruling class to the incoming one, understood by the whole community as final and binding. Every eight years, the Gumi Gaayo assembly , held under the sacred Odaa tree, reviews the era’s laws and blesses the incoming leadership. Contrast that with Kenya’s 2007 to 08 crisis, when a disputed result triggered ethnic violence that killed roughly 1,000 people and displaced 500,000, per HRW’s investigation . Ivory Coast saw a similar rupture in 2010 to 2011, leading to a civil war . In the Borana Gadaa system, succession is scripted years in advance.

In much of Africa, it is an open question resolved only after votes are contested. The Borana society has two broad blocks, the Sabboo Sadeen clan and the Goonaa Bal’aa clan, each with its own sub-clans. But the five Gogeessa that hold political authority cut across these clan lines — political identity and clan identity stay separate, so no single clan can capture the system. This fault line has broken many African elections.

The violence in Kenya in 2007 to 2008 was driven largely by ethnic mobilization, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies ( CSIS ) noting ethnicity as the main axis political elites mobilize around — turning elections into an ethnic census. Where political identity is inseparable from ethnicity, losing an election can feel like losing everything for a whole community. Gadaa’s design offers a template: build structures — party membership, constituencies, civil-service recruitment — that mix identities rather than reinforce them. Gadaa’s Gumi Gaayo assembly does far more than confirm who leads.

It reviews the era’s laws, arbitrates disputes, and holds outgoing leaders publicly accountable — through consultation among elders and councils of advisors (Hayyuu), not a ballot cast once every few years. Much of Africa’s politics concentrates almost all democratic energy into a single day. ITUC-Africa cataloged disputed results across Guinea, Togo, Sudan, Burundi, Burkina Faso, Egypt, Comoros, Tanzania, and Rwanda in 2010 alone — accountability between elections proved far weaker than the contest itself. Robust democracies need standing institutions — independent courts, electoral commissions, a free press and community dispute-resolution bodies — that keep working every day of the cycle. The Abbaa Gadaa — the topmost Borana Leader — never rules alone.

He operates alongside the Hayyuu council of advisors, the Abbaa Seera responsible for law, and the ritual authority of the Qaalluu — a deliberately decentralized structure, as one account puts it, designed to stop any office from concentrating too much power. Across Africa, the opposite dominates. A 2026 survey found rulers such as Cameroon’s Paul Biya (in power since 1982), Equatorial Guinea’s Teodoro Obiang Nguema Obiang (since 1979) and Congo’s Sassou Nguesso (since 1979) have systematically dismantled the checks meant to constrain them. In each case, the presidency grew larger than the constitution meant to contain it.

When power is distributed across councils, courts, and customary bodies, no single leader’s ambition can capture the whole state. Borana layers its conflict resolution: The Kora Gossa handles local clan disputes, the Gumi Gaayo settles national matters, and Boran Haraamu Koo’puu Rules — a form of social exclusion — is reserved for those who break the community’s deepest trust. Modern West Africa shows what happens when such mediation is absent. Since 2020, the Sahel has seen a wave of takeovers — Mali, Guinea, Burkina Faso, Niger, Gabon — linked to deteriorating security and falling accountability in the years before each coup.

The lesson is not that customary courts should replace constitutions, but that no state can survive on election-day mechanisms alone — it needs everyday channels of mediation to build citizens’ trust. Borana Gadaa’s institutions are inseparable from Borana culture. The Odaa tree is both a meeting place and a living symbol of continuity across generations. Knowledge of the system’s history — including a documented line of more than 72 Abbaa Gadaa — is preserved and transmitted by oral historians. Governance needs more than law and procedure — it needs cultural memory, shared symbols, and inclusive channels through which groups historically shut out of power, especially women, can still be heard.

African leaders don’t need to build Odaa trees or revive age-grade systems to learn from the Borana Gadaa. They need its underlying logic: time limits built into institutions, leaders prepared long before office, structures that cut across ethnic lines, power distributed across bodies, and dialogue running continuously rather than waiting for crisis.

pages.text: A free media is both a cornerstone of democracy and one of its strongest safeguards. It informs citizens, holds power to account, exposes corruption and strengthens security. A recent report we commissioned on the safety of journalists in the UK found 79% said they felt able to work freely, citing our history of democracy, free speech and an independent press. In contrast, 13% noted restrictions, a percentage we are committed to reducing. As co-chair of the Media Freedom Coalition, the UK will champion independent, pluralistic media.

We thank ODIHR and the Representative on Freedom of the Media for their work, urge participating States to uphold the 2018 Milan Decision on the Safety of Journalists. Yet within the OSCE region, journalists are threatened, detained, exiled and killed. Outlets face censorship, abusive legal action and financial pressure. Women journalists face targeted abuse. And disinformation erodes trust. Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine has shown the connection between media freedom and security. Journalists and aid volunteers near the frontline face risks to their safety, particularly from drones. Civilians must never be targeted, and Russia must distinguish between civilian and military objects under international humanitarian law.

In Ukrainian territory occupied by Russia, independent media face systematic repression. At least 26 Ukrainian journalists remain in Russian captivity. The UK calls for the immediate release of all journalists and media workers held by Russia, and accountability for attacks upon them. We support Ukrainian media, including Hromadske Radio. And we continue to condemn attacks and counter Russian information warfare. We remain concerned by democratic backsliding in Georgia. We condemn politically motivated detentions, including Mzia Amaglobeli, and call for the immediate release of those detained. Georgia should reverse repressive legislation and engage with independent experts deployed under the OSCE Moscow Mechanism.

The UK will not tolerate foreign states targeting critics, including journalists, on British soil. Journalists in exile must be able to work safely. Through the Media Freedom Coalition, we will pursue advocacy, share expertise, address threats to women journalists, support sustainable public-interest media, and confront the risks of artificial intelligence. OSCE officeholders, States, journalists and civil society must use the organisation’s mechanisms. Journalists must work without fear: when independent voices are silenced, disinformation spreads, corruption flourishes and democracies become less secure. Those who tell the truth must be protected, not punished. In an age of weaponised information, independent journalism has never mattered more.

pages.text: Homeowners across England will gain a clearer picture of their property’s flood risk under plans unveiled by the Government and Flood Re today (Tuesday 13 October 2026). New Flood Performance Certificates (FPCs) will be piloted to provide clear, standardised information on flood risk and resilience, reflecting the steps taken to protect them and where further action is needed. The goal is for FPCs to be a trusted source of information, similar to how Energy Performance Certificates are for energy. They will pilot approaches such as a ‘Flood Performance Rating’, which breaks a property’s flood risk down to categories such as exposure, characteristics and resistance.

This will draw on flood risk information already available through the ‘Check Your Flood Risk’ service, covering risks such as rivers and surface water. By helping people understand their vulnerabilities and how they can be addressed, FPCs are intended to drive greater uptake of practical resilience measures and support more climate-resilient communities. Household can invest in items, like self-closing air bricks, flood resilient kitchens and flood barriers. Being introduced by Flood Re, work on pilots to test the certificates will start this year in areas at risk of flooding, with a growing number of pilots also taking place throughout 2027 and beyond.

Flood Re’s ambition is for app-based flood self-assessments to become routine, helping people understand their individual risk, take steps to mitigate it, and in time have these actions recognised by their insurers. Working closely with homeowners, insurers and lenders, the pilots will test how resilience information can be assessed, communicated and recognised in a way that is useful for all users. Where homeowners take action to make their properties more resilient, such as installing flood barriers or water resilient flooring, this will be reflected in the assessment. If a property’s resilience can be improved, the certificate will make this clear and help identify where action is needed.

FPCs will aid insurers and lenders by providing access to more consistent, comparable information and support positive impact on the affordability and availability of insurance where action taken to improve flood resilience is sufficient to improve an insurers assessment of the flood risk. Earlier this year, the government and Flood Re unveiled plans to ensure flood insurance remains fair, affordable and sustainable, while accelerating action to improve flood resilience across the nation. This includes more than halving premiums for contents cover policies in Council Tax Bands A and B, to £25, from April 2027.

This change is intended to support lower-income households and renters, with insurers expected to pass these savings on to customers. This week also marks the Environment Agency’s Flood Action Week, running from 12 to 18 October. It encourages people to prepare for flooding by taking proactive steps such as knowing their flood risk, preparing a flood plan, and getting flood warnings. The Environment Agency maintains 260 mobile pumps, including 17 ultra-high-volume pumps, along with 25 kilometres of temporary barriers ready to be deployed wherever they are needed.
They also operate a 24/7 response to flooding emergencies, with 600 people on call at any one time and plans in place to escalate its response when needed.

pages.text: As announced in the Regulation on Political Advertising , which entered into full application one year ago on 10 October 2025, the Repository will support transparency and accountability in online political advertising. Once fully operational, the Repository will enable publishers to comply with the transparency requirements set down by the Regulation. It will also facilitate the work of interested entities such as researchers or journalists in scrutinising the political advertising landscape. The Repository will store transparency notices relating to political advertisements.

These notices provide information on who is behind an advertisement, including the sponsor, controlling entity and paying entity, as well as the amounts spent on the advertisement and the wider campaign of which it forms part. It will also include information on the source and origin of funding, including if it is public or private and if it originates from inside or outside the Union, the dissemination period, and the use of targeting or ad-delivery techniques based on personal data, including meaningful information on the use of AI systems for targeting or ad-delivery.

The Regulation established the Repository as the platform where political advertising publishers make online political advertisements and related transparency notices available for public scrutiny, research and oversight. Therefore, it will allow users to identify advertisements, access permanent URLs where available, and consult the information contained in transparency notices. The pilot version of the European Repository is available for voluntary use from 12 October 2026. The date of the official deployment of the Repository will be announced on the website sufficiently in advance to allow publishers to undertake preparations and familiarise themselves with the new standards.

The obligations relating to the European Repository will only become applicable as of the date of its official deployment. As regards the application of the Regulation on Political Advertising, the Network of national contact points serves as a platform for regular exchange of information, best practices and structured cooperation between competent Member State authorities and the Commission on all aspects of the Regulation. Moreover, an Expert group of providers of political advertising services has been established by the Commission to monitor and collect practical feedback on the application of the Regulation. The Expert group has been closely involved in the development of the pilot version of the Repository.

An Implementation Dialogue on the application of the Political Advertising Regulation will be hosted by Commissioner Michael McGrath on 4 November in Brussels. The dialogue allows stakeholders to exchange views with the Commissioner, share initial experiences with the application of the Regulation, and explore measures to support, facilitate and improve its application. pages.text: As this is the first meeting since the 10th of August, I extend our condolences to the people of Colombia for losses suffered in the earthquake of that day. Making peace is not easy, as every country on this Council knows. Significant challenges remain, and new challenges arise throughout the duration of any and every peace agreement. In Colombia, new and emerging armed groups continue to threaten communities, former combatants, and human rights defenders. Thirteen peace signatories have been killed so far in 2026.

The proliferation of armed groups both hinders implementation of Colombia’s Peace Agreement and reflects the need for its full and rapid implementation, including through restoring effective state presence as the minister said, across territories formerly under the influence of the FARC. At the same time, Colombia’s Peace Agreement has successfully secured the demobilization of one of the largest and most active guerilla groups. More than 11,000 former combatants remain demobilized, enrolled in reintegration programs, and committed to the Peace Agreement. So as we approach the Agreement’s 10th anniversary, the United Kingdom remains committed to its full implementation.

We welcome the Government of Colombia’s decision to uphold the constitutional and legal obligations arising from Colombia’s Peace Agreement. We note the Government’s ongoing review and hope that it will strengthen the institutional architecture and funding for the Peace Agreement, and ensure that the Agreement and its implementation architecture serves the needs of the communities most affected by the conflict. The next five years – the final five years – will be critical. We encourage the Government to use Colombia’s Peace Agreement and its provisions as part of an overall security framework.

To tackle the drivers of the conflict, build effective state presence at the same time as taking security and anti-narcotics measures. And we look to these measures to prioritise protection of vulnerable communities including Afro-Colombian, indigenous peoples, and children. The United Kingdom will continue to champion peacebuilding on the ground at local levels because we see that sustainable peace and security can only be achieved by involving civilians and survivors most affected by conflict. That working with civil society and listening to the voices of communities is important. And that women and girls face risks that need effective and sustained protection measures.

The United Kingdom sees the UN Verification Mission as continuing to be an essential tool for sustaining peace in Colombia. We look forward to presenting a draft resolution for consideration to this Council which would renew the mandate of the Mission. And look forward to discussing it with the Government of Colombia. As we look ahead to the final five years, our shared commitment to peace in Colombia should remain unwavering, bringing together all to support the full implementation of Colombia’s Peace Agreement and secure lasting peace for all Colombians.

pages.text: On Saturday, October 5, 2024, a Memorandum of Collaboration (MOC) was signed in Dhaka between the Wage Earners Welfare Board and Malaysia's PERKESO, regarding the expansion of the labor market in Malaysia. Image via Wikipedia by Press Information Department of Bangladesh. Public Domain. Officials in both Bangladesh and Malaysia’s have made repeated attempts to reform the countries’ labour migration relationship, leading to numerous suspensions and reopenings over more than three decades. However, on August 30, 2026, Bangladesh’s State Minister for Local Government, Rural Development and Cooperatives, Mir Shahe Alam, announced that Malaysia would recruit around 200,000 Bangladeshi workers over six months, with departures expected to begin in late September.

He also referred to a plan to send 10,000 workers without requiring them to bear migration costs. Two days later, however, Malaysia’s government spokesperson Fahmi Fadzil clarified that the figure of 200,000 workers did not represent an official government position. The clarification introduced fresh uncertainty over the scale and timing of the recruitment drive. The mixed signals came as the two countries were trying to reset a labour migration corridor that has faced repeated allegations of excessive recruitment fees, syndication and worker exploitation.

Bangladesh first entered into an agreement with Malaysia for the systematic transfer of labour in 1992, followed by another agreement in 1994 that provided for the recruitment of 50,000 workers annually, mainly for the construction sector. Between 1992 and 1998, around 307,000 Bangladeshi workers were issued permits to work in Malaysia. But recruitment was halted in 1997 amid a rise in unauthorised migration. During that period, local brokers could charge workers between USD 2,000 (approximately BDT 245,700) and USD 3,000 (approximately BDT 368,600) for authorised migration.

In an effort to reduce recruitment malpractice and costs, the two governments turned to a government-to-government model ( G2G model ) in 2012. The programme initially aimed to recruit around 30,000 Bangladeshi workers for Malaysia’s palm-oil sector. More than 1.4 million people registered and workers were selected through a lottery system. The G2G arrangement substantially reduced migration costs, but it struggled to meet its recruitment targets. The system was later replaced by the G2G Plus arrangement. Under the model introduced in 2016, Malaysia selected only 10 Bangladeshi recruiting agencies.

Although the agreed migration cost was around BDT 37,000-40,000 (approximately USD 300 to USD 325), later reports put the amount actually paid by workers at an average of around BDT 300,000 to 400,000 (approximately USD 2,450 to USD 3,260). Allegations of syndication, high costs and other irregularities eventually led Malaysia to suspend recruitment again in 2018. Recruitment resumed following a new memorandum of understanding signed in December 2021. Between 2022 and 2024, 476,672 Bangladeshi workers were sent to Malaysia through 101 recruiting agencies.

But by June 2024, the labour market had again closed to new Bangladeshi recruits amid concerns over high migration costs and worker exploitation. Against this history of repeated closed and reopened borders, the latest attempt to reset recruitment has revived a familiar question: whether the new arrangement can reduce the financial burden on workers and prevent the problems that undermined earlier recruitment systems. On August 28, 2026, Bangladesh’s Ministry of Expatriates’ Welfare and Overseas Employment outlined a broader recruitment arrangement involving 338 entities. Malaysia had directly selected 25 recruiting agencies, while 312 others were approved to work as associates.

The state-run Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited, or BOESL, was also included. Under the same arrangement, Malaysia had agreed in principle to take 10,000 workers on a zero-cost basis . Prospective migrants were also warned not to make payments, undergo medical examinations or hand over their passports until formal instructions were issued. That warning stands out against the record of the previous recruitment cycle. In July 2026, Bangladesh revoked the licences of 49 recruiting agencies over alleged syndication and irregularities linked to Malaysia-bound recruitment.

The Anti-Corruption Commission alleged that agencies under investigation had sent 267,276 workers to Malaysia and collected more than BDT 45.45 billion (approximately USD 370 million) in excess fees. The government-approved recruitment cost was BDT 78,990 (approximately USD 645), yet investigators alleged that some workers were charged as much as five times that amount. Concerns over high recruitment costs have continued into the new cycle, with industry sources warning that migration expenses could exceed BDT 600,000 (approximately USD 4,900). The financial burden is not limited to the Malaysia corridor.

Bangladesh’s Labour Force Survey 2024 found that migrant workers spent an average of BDT 463,000 (approximately USD 3,778 ) on recruitment. With average monthly earnings of BDT 42,599 (approximately USD 348), recovering that expense took about 10.9 months on average. For some families, however, the financial loss begins even before a worker leaves Bangladesh. For a 22-year-old worker originally from Sherpur, Bangladesh, the financial loss began with a job abroad that he never reached. Speaking to Global Voices by phone and asking to remain anonymous, he said he began preparing to migrate to Malaysia around 2024 after hearing about work opportunities through a local intermediary.

By the time the process stalled, his family had spent around BDT 500,000 (approximately USD 4,079). The money came from their savings, the sale of land and loans — around BDT 220,000 (approximately USD 1,795) of which were borrowed at interest. The payments were made in stages for visa processing, medical costs and other expenses. Much of the process was handled through a local intermediary rather than directly with a recruiting agency, and the worker said he did not receive receipts for all of the money he paid. “At first they said it would take two or three months, but six or seven months passed.

Whenever I asked for an update, the intermediary gave a different answer but never gave me a clear one. I had already done the medical and submitted my passport. Eventually they told me the Malaysian market had closed and there was nothing more they could do.” By then, however, the full amount had already been paid, leaving him and his family with the financial burden. “I thought I would go to Malaysia, earn money, and repay the loan. But I could not go. I got some of the money back, but they still have not returned the rest. Whenever I call, they just say, ‘Give us some more time.’

I do not know how long I am supposed to keep waiting. I am still here, but I am still paying off the debt I took to go abroad.” The consequences also reached the rest of the household. His mother, who also spoke to Global Voices by phone and asked to remain anonymous, said, “My husband died a long time ago. We only had a small piece of land, so I sold it. I also borrowed money with interest and somehow managed the rest for my son. I thought that if he could go abroad and earn well, we would repay everything. But he could not go.

Now we still have to keep paying the interest, whether we have enough for food or not.” The family’s experience sits within a broader pattern of high recruitment costs and debt among Bangladeshis seeking work in Malaysia. Research by Verité , an independent nonprofit organization advancing fair labor worldwide, on the Bangladesh–Malaysia migration corridor found that workers paid an average of about USD 5,000 (approximately BDT 614,400) in recruitment-related costs, often financing the journey through multiple loans. Among the workers surveyed , 73 percent spent at least half of their monthly salary on recruitment debt, while 43 percent reported wage deception.

The role of intermediaries has also been identified as a major driver of those costs. An International Organization for Migration (IOM) study on recruitment practices in Bangladesh found that aspiring migrants often rely on sub-agents and informal intermediaries because they have little direct contact with recruiting agencies or do not fully understand the formal process. The study identified reducing the unauthorised involvement of such intermediaries as a key step towards lowering migration costs. A separate IOM study on migrant debt found that limited information about official migration channels can push prospective workers towards intermediaries who charge high fees.

It also identified limited access to formal finance and legal remedies as factors that can deepen migrant indebtedness. As Bangladesh and Malaysia move towards restarting recruitment, key details of the process remain unsettled. By September 30, 2026, the Bangladesh High Commission in Kuala Lumpur had begun attesting job-demand letters, but the government had yet to announce the final recruitment cost, departure timeline, or full procedure. Expatriates’ Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury said an official announcement would be made soon. The structure of the new arrangement has also drawn criticism from within the recruitment industry.

Some Bangladesh Association of International Recruiting Agencies ( BAIRA ) members argued that the 312 associate agencies should have direct access to Malaysia’s Foreign Workers Centralised Management System rather than relying on the 25 principal agencies to process workers. Other recruiters rejected concerns about renewed syndication, saying associate agencies could still obtain job demand and recruit workers. In November 2025, UN human rights experts expressed renewed concern over the continued exploitation, deception and deepening debt bondage of Bangladeshi migrant workers in Malaysia. They called on both governments to investigate reported abuses, provide effective remedies including restitution and debt relief, strengthen oversight of recruitment practices and cooperate to dismantle exploitative recruitment networks.

The recruitment corridor has also faced repeated suspensions amid recurring allegations of syndication, excessive recruitment costs and worker exploitation. Malaysia suspended recruitment of Bangladeshi workers in 2018 following controversy surrounding the limited-agency system, and again in June 2024 amid concerns over excessive migration costs and workers arriving without jobs. The repeated disruptions have renewed concerns over whether restricted recruitment arrangements can ensure transparency and protect workers from exploitation. Meanwhile, the Malaysian government has warned agencies not to collect money or passports before formal instructions are issued.

Migration researcher Shariful Hasan also told The Daily Star that any reopening should clearly establish who controls recruitment, how much workers are required to pay and who is accountable when problems arise. Bangladesh and Malaysia have made several government-level agreements over the years, but problems such as syndication, excessive recruitment costs and human rights abuses remain unresolved. Remittances are a major source of support for Bangladesh’s economy, yet migrant workers continue to bear significant human and financial costs. This highlights the need for urgent reforms by both governments that are transparent and centred on the rights and protection of workers.

pages.text: Anxiety and depression are the most common mental disorders. Such conditions can affect all aspects of our lives, including relationships with family, friends and community. They can result from or lead to problems at school and at work. And the economic consequences are substantial. According to a 2023 study, nearly half of Europeans declared having experienced an emotional or psychological problem such as feeling depressed or anxious. World Mental Health Day on October 10 serves as a reminder that good mental health is important and how we can prioritise it in our lives.

This year’s theme ‘Lived experiences heard: real voices, real change’ stresses how conversations about mental health make a difference. At EU level, mental health is already a health priority. In 2023, it adopted a comprehensive approach to mental health , which is helping EU countries and interested groups to take swift action to deal with mental health challenges. It focuses on prevention, addressing behavioural risk factors and social, environmental, and commercial conditions that play their part in the development of mental health disorders. In addition, of particular concern today are the pressures of the digital sphere and social media on our mental health.

Modern platforms are highly addictive and designed to keep us engaged for as long as possible, particularly children. EU laws and initiatives are already tackling addictive design, excessive screen time, exposure to illegal content, cyberbullying, and cyberviolence. Last month, the EU also proposed the EU KIDS Act , based on the recommendations from the Special Panel on Child Safety Online . The proposal seeks to prevent access to social media platforms by children under the age of 13 and sets an EU-wide minimum age for minors to open an account of their own. It’s not only the EU and national governments addressing mental health issues. We can all play our part in improving people’s mental well-being. On October 10, take the time to listen.

pages.text: The UK is set to deepen its work with the international Jewish community to stamp out antisemitism, following a UK-hosted meeting coordinating efforts against rising antisemitic behaviour and strengthening support for Jewish people everywhere. The Foreign Secretary today hosted the J7 Global Task Force in London, bringing together national Jewish organisations and representatives from the seven countries with the largest Jewish populations outside Israel. Participants discussed practical ways to tackle antisemitism, strengthen international coordination and share effective approaches to protecting Jewish communities. This includes the UK also agreeing to host a future J7 Ministerial-level meeting on antisemitism.

The meeting comes as the J7’s latest annual report found that 2025 was the deadliest year for Jews living outside Israel since 1994, with the UK among the countries that recorded an increase in antisemitic incidents. The UK is working with international partners to deepen cooperation against antisemitism, building on action already being taken domestically to protect Jewish communities and tackle anti-Jewish hatred. “Antisemitism has no place in our society. Jewish communities must be able to live freely and safely, without fear of discrimination, abuse or violence. “The rise in antisemitic incidents across a number of countries demands a coordinated international response.

Today’s discussion helped identify practical ways that governments, communities and international partners can work together to tackle antisemitism and share what works. “The UK is committed to leading international efforts to combat antisemitism wherever it occurs.” The meeting builds on wider UK action to tackle antisemitism. Alongside measures to strengthen protection for Jewish communities domestically, the UK is working with international partners to coordinate global action, share best practice and ensure Jewish communities can live safely and confidently wherever they are.

pages.text: A new film, produced in partnership with Aardman, the Environment Agency and East Sussex County Council, has been launched today (Monday 12 October) to help people understand their flood risk and the support available to protect their homes and families. Its launch comes as part of Flood Action Week, the Environment Agency’s national campaign encouraging people to check their flood risk, sign up for flood warnings, and take simple steps to protect their property ahead of a heightened risk of flooding this winter.

Building on previous flood resilience animations, including Missy’s Tale and Darcy’s Tale, all directed by Åsa Lucander at multi-award-winning studio Aardman, this latest film supports the Environment Agency’s ongoing work to help communities understand their flood risk and take action to protect themselves, their property and their livelihoods. As the nation marks Flood Action Week, the Environment Agency has launched ‘Flood Action Online’, a one-stop shop for flood advice.

This will benefit millions of families across England by bringing together actionable guidance and easy access to Met Office weather alerts during incidents, this will support homeowners in becoming more resilient to flooding, including through practical changes like property flood resilience measures. The government has also set a new commitment to safeguard 200,000 properties from flooding, delivering a total economic benefit of £27.9 billion in avoided damage as communities gain better protection and growth is delivered in every postcode.

The film was developed by Blue Heart Project, led by East Sussex County Council, and funded through the £200 million Flood and Coastal Innovation Programme that is managed by the Environment Agency. In the film, flooding arrives unexpectedly and turns Missy and Stanley’s pet basket into a makeshift raft. As they travel through flooded streets and past local landmarks, Missy and Stanley learn how dramatically flooding can change familiar places. The video is available to watch on YouTube now: Missy and Stanley’s Tale by Aardman - YouTube

In Mozambique , freedom of expression is regulated by the Law on the Right to Information No. 34/2014 , a constitutionally guaranteed right under Article 48 of the Constitution of the Republic of Mozambique . However, for many young people, speaking publicly about corruption, inequality, police violence, or accountability continues to carry risk, showing the gap between the promises of democracy and actual daily experience. In music, for example, this contradiction is clear.

Over the past two decades, hip-hop has become a key space for urban youth to voice social criticism, particularly in the capital city, Maputo . More than simply a musical genre, hip-hop became a way of documenting the concerns of a generation that grew up with, on one hand, political democratization and multipartyism from the early 1990s , but on the other, high youth unemployment, economic inequalities, and growing distrust in public institutions led by the ruling FRELIMO party. Through musical narratives, groups like GPRO and artists like Azagaia created a language that reflected people’s daily experiences in public and institutional spaces.

Perhaps the question Azagaia poses in the song “ O ciclo da Censura ” (Cycle of Censorship) remains relevant: “Who said that in this country there is freedom of expression?” This is not just a provocative artistic comment. It is a reflection on the material and political conditions that determine who can speak, about what, and with what consequences. Mozambican youth have been reinventing ways of participating politically. While for many years citizenship was strongly associated with political parties and state organizations, today it also flows through other organizations such as feminist collectives like the Woman’s Forum , digital platforms for monitoring local governance , cultural associations, and artistic initiatives.

This change points to a generation that does not accept politics being limited to elections, and demands the right to continually participate in the shaping of public spaces. However, these new forms of participation often conflict with authorities that continue to view protest as a threat to public order. One of the most striking events happened in 2016, when feminist organizations took to the streets to protest the banning of miniskirts in state schools . The measure was presented as a response to sexual harassment, but it implied that female students’ clothing choices were the cause of the harm they suffered.

By holding the girls accountable instead of the aggressors, the debate revealed something deeper: the dispute over control of the female body and the right of young women to define their own identity. During the demonstrations, the Spanish activist Eva Anadón Moreno was detained and subsequently expelled from Mozambique for participating in the protest. In recent years, censorship in Mozambique has rarely come in the form of explicit prohibitions. However, that does not mean that fear and self-censorship are entirely absent. In a 2010 interview, Azagaia observed that the biggest obstacle to freedom of expression in Mozambique was not necessarily direct police intimidation, but rather economic precarity.

When many job opportunities depend, directly or indirectly, on relationships with established power structures, public criticism can put people at risk. This results in what could be called the “economy of silence.” Journalists avoid certain topics, artists moderate what they say, public officials keep their opinions quiet, and young activists learn that words can carry a high cost. Freedom then ceases to be merely a legal issue and becomes a matter of survival. In this context, protest music takes on a particular political value. It breaks the collective silence and develops communities of recognition-building, where experiences of injustice find language, memory, and solidarity.

The Mozambican Constitution affirms the right of all citizens to freedom of expression and opinion. But a democracy is not measured only by rights on paper, but also by the real conditions in which they can be exercised. The mirage of freedom lies in this contradiction: Citizens are asked to believe they can speak freely, while informal mechanisms of surveillance, stigmatization, and exclusion limit who can participate in public space. It is not necessary to prohibit all voices; it is enough to make the costs of dissent intimidatingly high, such as, for example, the increase of telecommunications tariffs above the real cost .

In this context, the youth activism symbolizes this ambivalence. They amplify historically marginalized voices and make them more visible. The greater the capacity of an artist, activist, or youth collective to mobilize people, the greater the risk of intimidation, disinformation, or economic isolation. Despite the challenges, youth continue to create new forms of political hope. Art, music, and digital activism show that citizenship is not just a legal status, but a daily practice of participation, imagination, and resistance.

The real challenge of protecting Mozambicans is not just freedom of expression as written in the constitution, but creating conditions for everybody to exercise it without fear of economic, social, or political reprisals. The fundamental question for Mozambique is not just whether young people can speak, but whether they can speak without putting their safety, their job, or their ability to participate in public life at risk.
